concepts.name: Carbon Cycle: Major Reservoirs and Flux Rates
key_dimensions: Relative sizes of reservoirs: lithosphere > ocean > atmosphere > biosphere — and why this order matters
Flux rates between reservoirs (fast cycle vs. slow cycle) and residence time in each reservoir
Ocean as both a source and sink — carbonate-bicarbonate buffering system
UPSC trap: distinguishing between carbon stock and carbon flux — a large reservoir does not mean a large flux

concepts.name: Photosynthesis and Respiration as Carbon Cycle Drivers
key_dimensions: Gross Primary Production (GPP) vs. Net Primary Production (NPP) vs. Net Ecosystem Production (NEP)
Why the biosphere is considered 'carbon neutral' over annual cycles — GPP ≈ total respiration
Seasonal fluctuation of atmospheric CO2 (Keeling Curve) and its linkage to terrestrial photosynthesis
UPSC trap: NPP is NOT the carbon sequestered — it is GPP minus plant respiration; carbon sequestration requires NEP to be positive

concepts.name: Role of Oceans in the Carbon Cycle: Biological and Solubility Pumps
key_dimensions: Solubility pump: CO2 dissolves more in cold polar waters — thermohaline circulation transports carbon to deep ocean
Biological pump: phytoplankton fix CO2; dead organic matter sinks as 'marine snow' sequestering carbon in deep ocean
Ocean acidification as a feedback: increased CO2 → carbonic acid → reduced pH → impairs biological pump
UPSC trap: oceans absorb ~25% of anthropogenic CO2 but this is slowing as oceans warm — net sink capacity is declining

concepts.name: Terrestrial Carbon Sinks: Forests, Soils, and Wetlands
key_dimensions: Soil organic carbon (SOC) — largest terrestrial carbon pool, exceeds atmospheric + vegetation carbon combined
Peatlands and mangroves as disproportionately large 'blue carbon' and 'brown carbon' sinks per unit area
Permafrost carbon feedback: thawing releases CH4 and CO2 — a positive feedback loop to climate change
UPSC trap: deforestation is a source while afforestation is a sink, but old-growth forests sequester more per year than young plantations

concepts.name: Methane (CH4) in the Carbon Cycle: Sources, Sinks, and Climate Significance
key_dimensions: Natural sources: wetlands, termites, oceans; Anthropogenic sources: rice paddies, livestock (enteric fermentation), landfills, fossil fuels
CH4 Global Warming Potential (GWP): ~84x CO2 over 20 years, ~28x over 100 years — why the timeframe matters for policy
Methanogenesis (anaerobic) vs. methanotrophy (aerobic bacteria consume CH4) — soils as both source and sink
UPSC trap: wetlands are the largest natural source of CH4 but also important carbon sinks — they are simultaneously source and sink depending on conditions

concepts.name: Nitrogen Cycle: Key Processes and Responsible Organisms
key_dimensions: Five key processes: nitrogen fixation → ammonification → nitrification → assimilation → denitrification — sequence and location in ecosystem
Organisms responsible: Rhizobium (symbiotic), Azotobacter/Cyanobacteria (free-living fixers), Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter (nitrifiers), Pseudomonas (denitrifiers)
UPSC trap: nitrification (NH4+ → NO2- → NO3-) is an aerobic process; denitrification (NO3- → N2) is anaerobic — confused frequently
Anammox (anaerobic ammonium oxidation) — recently discovered process, significant for oceanic nitrogen loss

concepts.name: Biological Nitrogen Fixation (BNF): Mechanisms and Ecological Significance
key_dimensions: Nitrogenase enzyme: requires anaerobic conditions even in aerobic organisms — leghemoglobin in root nodules maintains microaerobic environment
Energetic cost of BNF: 16 ATP per N2 fixed — why legumes invest heavily in photosynthate to support Rhizobium
Asymbiotic fixers: Azotobacter (aerobic, free soil), Clostridium (anaerobic, free soil), Anabaena/Nostoc (cyanobacteria in water bodies and rice paddies)
UPSC trap: all nitrogen-fixing organisms are prokaryotes — no eukaryote can directly fix N2; the Azolla-Anabaena symbiosis is used in rice cultivation

concepts.name: Denitrification and Nitrogen Loss from Ecosystems
key_dimensions: Conditions favoring denitrification: waterlogged/anaerobic soils, high NO3- concentration, available carbon source
End products: N2O (potent GHG, GWP ~265x CO2 over 100 years) and N2 — ratio depends on O2 levels and pH
Agricultural significance: waterlogged paddy soils and over-irrigation cause nitrogen loss reducing fertilizer efficiency
UPSC trap: denitrification is the primary return pathway of nitrogen to atmosphere — without it, N would accumulate in soils/water; it is a 'completing' step of the cycle

concepts.name: The Nitrogen Cascade and Reactive Nitrogen Pollution
key_dimensions: Reactive nitrogen (Nr) definition: all N forms except N2 — includes NH3, NOx, N2O, NO3-, organic N
Nitrogen cascade concept: one Nr molecule can cause multiple sequential environmental harms (eutrophication → hypoxia → acidification → ozone depletion)
Sources of Nr: Haber-Bosch process (synthetic fertilizers) and fossil fuel combustion — humans have doubled pre-industrial Nr creation
UPSC trap: the Haber-Bosch process is considered both humanity's greatest agricultural achievement AND a major driver of environmental degradation — dual nature frequently tested

concepts.name: Eutrophication: Mechanism, Consequences, and Linkage to N and P Cycles
key_dimensions: Process: nutrient enrichment → algal bloom → decomposer bacteria consume O2 → hypoxia/anoxia → dead zones
Limiting nutrient distinction: phosphorus typically limits freshwater eutrophication; nitrogen typically limits marine eutrophication (Liebig's Law of Minimum)
Cultural eutrophication vs. natural eutrophication — human acceleration through agriculture and sewage discharge
UPSC trap: eutrophication increases biological productivity but DECREASES biodiversity — a counterintuitive relationship frequently tested

concepts.name: Phosphorus Cycle: Why It Has No Atmospheric Component
key_dimensions: Phosphorus cycle is a sedimentary cycle — no significant gaseous phase unlike C and N cycles; this makes it the 'slowest' major nutrient cycle
Sources: weathering of phosphate rocks (apatite); the cycle is essentially one-directional on human timescales — lost to ocean sediments
Phosphorus as the ultimate limiting nutrient over geological time — why P availability constrains long-term ecosystem productivity
UPSC trap: unlike N (which can be fixed from atmosphere), depleted soil P cannot be replenished naturally at human timescales — peak phosphorus is a real resource concern

concepts.name: Phosphorus in Soils: Fixation, Availability, and Mycorrhizal Role
key_dimensions: Phosphorus fixation in soils: P binds tightly to Fe and Al oxides in acidic soils, and to Ca in alkaline soils — most soil P is unavailable to plants
Mycorrhizal fungi dramatically increase plant P uptake by extending effective root surface area — up to 1000x increase
Phosphatase enzymes released by plant roots and microbes mineralize organic P — biological availability pathway
UPSC trap: unlike N and K, phosphorus does NOT leach easily in soils (it gets fixed) but CAN cause water pollution through surface runoff and erosion — a common confusion

concepts.name: Peak Phosphorus and Geopolitical Dimensions of P Scarcity
key_dimensions: Global phosphate rock reserves: concentrated in Morocco (~70% of world reserves) — geopolitical vulnerability for food security
Peak phosphorus concept: minable reserves may peak within 50-100 years; unlike oil, there is no substitute for P in agriculture
Circular economy solutions: recycling P from wastewater, sewage sludge, animal bones — struvite recovery technology
UPSC trap: India imports ~90% of its phosphatic fertilizer raw material — direct national food security implication often tested in economy-environment overlap questions

concepts.name: Carbon-Nitrogen-Phosphorus Stoichiometry: Redfield Ratio and Its Implications
key_dimensions: Redfield Ratio: C:N:P = 106:16:1 in marine phytoplankton — represents the 'ideal' ratio for ocean primary producers
Implications: if ocean N:P deviates from 16:1, it predicts whether N or P limits marine productivity in a given region
Terrestrial stoichiometry differs: C:N:P ratios in soils and plants vary widely, affecting decomposition rates and nutrient cycling speeds
UPSC trap: Redfield Ratio is a marine concept — its direct application to terrestrial or freshwater systems is an oversimplification; deviations indicate nutrient stress

concepts.name: Decomposition and Nutrient Mineralization: The Detritus Pathway
key_dimensions: Decomposition rate controlled by: temperature, moisture, oxygen availability, and C:N ratio of litter (high C:N = slow decomposition)
Immobilization vs. mineralization: when C:N > 30, microbes immobilize N (net N removal from soil); when C:N < 25, net N mineralization occurs
Soil food web: bacteria → protozoa → nematodes → arthropods — each trophic level releases nutrients through excretion
UPSC trap: adding straw (high C:N ~80:1) to soil can cause temporary nitrogen deficiency in crops as microbes immobilize soil N — a common agricultural trap question

concepts.name: Feedback Loops in Nutrient Cycles and Climate Change Interactions
key_dimensions: Positive feedbacks: permafrost thaw → C and N release → warming → more thaw; also, warming → increased decomposition → CO2 release
Negative feedbacks: CO2 fertilization effect — higher CO2 stimulates plant growth, increasing C uptake (but limited by N and P availability)
Nutrient-climate interactions: nitrogen deposition from air pollution can fertilize forests increasing C sequestration — unintended benefit of pollution
UPSC trap: CO2 fertilization effect is real but self-limiting — N and P become limiting nutrients as plants grow faster, so it cannot offset all fossil fuel emissions

concepts.name: Human Disruption of Nutrient Cycles: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Nitrogen: humans have doubled annual N fixation through Haber-Bosch and fossil fuels — most disrupted biogeochemical cycle
Phosphorus: mining and agricultural use has increased P flux to oceans 3-4x pre-industrial levels — disrupted but no atmospheric pathway for recovery
Carbon: atmospheric CO2 is 50% above pre-industrial levels — unprecedented rate of change in geological record (except mass extinction events)
UPSC trap: nitrogen cycle is considered more disrupted than carbon cycle in relative terms (doubling vs. 50% increase) — yet carbon gets more climate attention

concepts.name: Wetlands as Biogeochemical Hotspots: Multi-Nutrient Cycling
key_dimensions: Wetlands simultaneously: sequester carbon (peat formation), remove nitrogen (active denitrification), retain phosphorus (sediment binding)
Paradox: wetlands are the largest natural source of CH4 — the same anaerobic conditions that make them carbon sinks also produce methane
Ramsar Convention significance: recognizes wetlands' role in water purification = nutrient cycling services translated to policy
UPSC trap: draining wetlands for agriculture releases stored carbon (carbon source) AND eliminates nitrogen removal service AND increases flood risk — multiple ecosystem services lost simultaneously

concepts.name: Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) and Nitrous Oxide (N2O): Sources, Sinks, and Atmospheric Roles
key_dimensions: N2O sources: agricultural soils (largest), livestock, biomass burning, industrial processes — 60% of N2O emissions are agricultural
N2O dual role: greenhouse gas (GWP ~265) AND ozone-depleting substance — it is now the dominant ozone-depleting emission
NOx (NO + NO2) from fossil fuels: contributes to tropospheric ozone formation (bad ozone) and acid rain — different from N2O
UPSC trap: N2O destroys stratospheric ozone (bad) while NOx creates tropospheric ozone (also bad) — both are 'bad' but in different atmospheric layers and through different mechanisms

concepts.name: Blue Carbon: Coastal Ecosystems and Their Role in Carbon and Nutrient Cycling
key_dimensions: Blue carbon ecosystems: mangroves, seagrasses, salt marshes — sequester carbon at rates 2-4x greater per unit area than terrestrial forests
Mechanism: high productivity + waterlogged anaerobic soils slow decomposition — organic carbon accumulates in sediments for millennia
Nutrient cycling role: mangroves are efficient nitrogen and phosphorus filters between terrestrial and marine ecosystems — buffer coral reefs from eutrophication

UPSC trap: blue carbon per hectare is much higher than forests, but total global area is much smaller — absolute contribution is smaller but loss per hectare is catastrophically high; destruction reverses centuries of stored carbon
